context.heading: Asleep below deck
context.body: While pagan sailors cry to their gods, Jonah radam ("fell into a deep sleep"), the same verb used of Sisera collapsing in Judges 4:21. The captain's words, "Get up and call" (v. 6), echo God's own command in verse 2. A pagan sailor has to tell the prophet to pray.

context.heading: He says he fears the LORD
context.body: Jonah tells the sailors, "I fear the LORD", which this translation renders "I worship". It is true and ironic at once: he claims to fear the God he is running from. Meanwhile fear grows among the sailors (vv. 5, 10) until they "feared the LORD greatly" (v. 16), and offer Him sacrifices.

context.heading: A great fish, appointed
context.body: God manah ("appointed") a great fish, the same verb He will use for a plant, a worm and a wind (4:6–8). Hebrew says "great fish", not whale. Many Christians read Jonah as straightforward history, noting that Jesus speaks of it alongside real events (Matthew 12:40–42); others read it as an inspired teaching story. Both take its message as God's word.

theology.title: Maker of the sea
theology.body: Jonah's creed is correct: the LORD made "the sea and the dry land" (v. 9). The storm rises and falls at His word. He is not a local god of Israel who can be escaped by sailing west, but the Lord of every place and every nation (Psalm 139:7–10).

theology.title: Mercy reaches the outsiders
theology.body: The sailors try hard not to harm Jonah (v. 13), pray to the LORD and end up worshiping Him. God's mercy reaches foreigners even through His messenger's disobedience. It previews the whole book: God cares about people Jonah would rather avoid.

theology.title: Something greater than Jonah
theology.body: Jonah sleeps through a storm and must be thrown overboard for his own sin. Jesus also slept in a storm, then calmed it with a word (Mark 4:35–41). He said "something greater than Jonah is here" (Matthew 12:41): one who would give His life for the sins of others.

application.title: The ship is always available
application.body: Jonah found a ship ready to leave and paid the fare. An open door is not always God's direction; sometimes it is just an easy exit.
application.question: What open door are you treating as permission when it might be an escape?

application.title: Sleeping through it
application.body: While everyone else panicked, Jonah slept. Numbness can be a way of running without moving.
application.question: What are you using, whether a screen, work or sleep, to avoid hearing something?

application.title: Your choices have passengers
application.body: The sailors lost their cargo and nearly their lives because of one man's flight. Private disobedience rarely stays private.
application.question: Who else is in the boat with the choice you are making right now?

context.heading: Down to the pit
context.body: Jonah sank to "the roots of the mountains", with the earth's bars locked behind him. Shachat ("pit") is a common word for the grave. Chapter 1 was a steady going down; here, for the first time, the movement turns upward: "You raised my life."

context.heading: Holding on to vapor
context.body: "Worthless idols" is literally "vapors of emptiness". Hevel, the word Ecclesiastes uses for "meaningless", means a breath or mist. Those who cling to it let go of chesed, God's loyal love. The pagan sailors had just done the reverse, turning from their gods to the LORD.

context.heading: The fish obeys
context.body: The LORD "commanded the fish" and it spat Jonah onto dry land. The creature obeys at once, something the prophet has not yet managed. The scene is almost comic: the most powerful empire's capital waits while God returns His messenger to the beach.

theology.title: Salvation belongs to the LORD
theology.body: Jonah's confession, "Salvation is from the LORD" (v. 9), comes while he is still inside the fish. Rescue is God's gift, not a reward for good behavior. Revelation 7:10 echoes the same cry from the redeemed of every nation.

theology.title: The sign of Jonah
theology.body: Jesus said, "As Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth" (Matthew 12:40). Jewish counting treated part of a day as a day. Jesus' death and resurrection is the greater sign Jonah pointed to.

theology.title: Grace ahead of growth
theology.body: Jonah's prayer thanks God but never mentions Nineveh, and chapter 4 shows his heart has not changed. God rescues him anyway. His grace runs ahead of our maturity and then patiently works on what is left.

application.title: Borrowed words
application.body: Jonah's prayer is stitched together from psalms he already knew. When you have no words of your own, Scripture lends them.
application.question: Which psalm could you learn now so it is there when you are underwater?

application.title: Thanks before the shore
application.body: Jonah gave thanks while still inside the fish: rescued, but not yet out. Gratitude does not have to wait for a resolution.
application.question: What can you thank God for before your situation is resolved?

application.title: Name your vapors
application.body: Hevel is anything that looks solid but vanishes when grabbed: approval, savings, followers, a body that never ages.
application.question: What are you gripping so tightly that you have no hand free for God's loyal love?

context.heading: A second time
context.body: "The word of the LORD came to Jonah a second time", repeating the commission of 1:2 almost word for word. Shenit ("second") signals restoration. God did not find a replacement prophet; He reissued the call, as Jesus later did with Peter (John 21:15–19).

context.heading: Forty days
context.body: Jonah's message is five Hebrew words with no call to repent and no offer of mercy. Arbaim ("forty") is Scripture's number for a period of testing: the flood rains, Moses on the mountain, Israel's years in the wilderness. The forty days were a deadline, and also a window.

context.heading: Sackcloth, even for cattle
context.body: Saq ("sackcloth") was coarse goat-hair cloth worn in mourning. The king orders even animals to wear it (v. 8). The Greek historian Herodotus describes Persians including their horses in mourning rites, so the detail fits the wider world, though it sounds odd to us.

theology.title: Does God change His mind?
theology.body: God "relented" (v. 10). This is not fickleness. Many of His warnings are conditional, meant to bring people to repentance (Jeremiah 18:7–8). The king's "Who knows?" (v. 9) is the same hope the prophet Joel holds out to Israel (Joel 2:14).

theology.title: The Ninevites will testify
theology.body: Jesus said the men of Nineveh will rise at the judgment and condemn His generation, because they repented at Jonah's preaching and "something greater than Jonah is here" (Matthew 12:41). A reluctant prophet with a five-word sermon got a better response than the Son of God did from many.

theology.title: Judgment and mercy together
theology.body: God's threat against Nineveh was real, aimed at "the violence in his hands" (v. 8). His mercy was just as real. He is not soft on evil, and He is not eager to destroy. The cross shows both at once: sin judged and sinners spared (Romans 3:25–26).

application.title: Second chances come with assignments
application.body: God gave Jonah his old task back. Restoration did not mean an easier job; it meant the same one, done this time.
application.question: What assignment have you been hoping God would forget about?

application.title: Repentance from the top
application.body: The king left his throne, took off his robe and sat in ashes. The person with the most power went first.
application.question: Where in your home or work do you need to be the first to admit fault?

application.title: Nobody is too far gone
application.body: Nineveh was the last place an Israelite would expect to turn to God, and the whole city did. Our predictions about who will listen are often wrong.
application.question: Who have you quietly decided is too far gone to hear about God?

context.heading: A great evil to Jonah
context.body: Verse 1 literally says "it was evil to Jonah, a great evil". God had just turned from the ra'ah ("disaster") planned for Nineveh (3:10), and Jonah treats that mercy as a disaster of its own. The wordplay exposes how upside down his view had become.

context.heading: Burning anger
context.body: Charah means "to burn" with anger, and it appears three times (vv. 1, 4, 9). God answers His prophet's tantrum with a question, not a thunderbolt: "Have you any right to be angry?" Jonah's first complaint even quotes God's own goodness against Him.

context.heading: A plant, a worm, a wind
context.body: The qiqayon was a fast-growing plant, perhaps a castor-oil plant or a gourd; nobody is sure. God appoints the plant, then a worm, then a scorching wind, using the same verb as for the fish (1:17). He is staging an object lesson for one angry man.

theology.title: A God who reasons
theology.body: The book ends with a question, not a verdict (v. 11). God patiently argues with His sulking prophet, much like the father pleading with the older brother in Luke 15:25–32. He wants Jonah's heart, not just his obedience.

theology.title: Compassion for enemies
theology.body: Assyria would later destroy the northern kingdom of Israel (2 Kings 17:6), so Jonah's anger is understandable. Yet God cares for more than 120,000 people and even their cattle. He loved Nineveh while it was still an enemy, just as Christ died for us while we were God's enemies (Romans 5:10).

theology.title: Lord of the smallest things
theology.body: A plant, a worm and a morning wind all move at God's command. Nothing is too small for His attention, and He uses even minor discomforts to teach (Matthew 10:29–31). The God who steers empires also schedules a worm.

application.title: Angry at grace
application.body: Jonah loved mercy when it rescued him from the fish. He hated it when it reached people who had hurt his nation.
application.question: Whose forgiveness would honestly make you angry?

application.title: Upset about the wrong thing
application.body: Jonah grieved a shade plant more than a city of people. It is easy to get more upset about a cracked phone or a cancelled plan than about a neighbor far from God.
application.question: What small comfort do you get more upset about losing than people?

application.title: Finish the story yourself
application.body: The book never tells us how Jonah answered. The question is left open for each reader.
application.question: If God asked whether you have any right to your anger, what would you honestly say?
